content:
Finally time for deployment of my REST API, setting up automatic deployment when pushing to main. For this I use GitHub Actions and a Watchtower on DigitalOcean to poll for a new image on Docker Hub.
When pushing the project to GitHub it checks if it’s push or pull request to main.
Push:
Runs test and Maven builds the project as a fat jar and build a Docker image contain the jar and pushes it to Docker Hub. Pull request:
Runs test and Maven builds the project as a fat jar, but nothing is deployed. If a test fails, the process stops before the Docker steps, so a broken build never reaches the server.
On the DigitalOcean, Watchtower runs as a container next to the application. It polls Docker Hub for a new version of the image and, when one appears, pulls it and restarts the application container with the same settings from docker-compose.yml.
It’s secured using secrets on both ends, the .env and GitHub secrets holds values needed for the process. GitHub holds values needed for the build like JWT settings used for tests and Docker Hub username and a secret access token for the push the image. Everything needed when the application is running on DigitalOcean is kept in .env, so the image itself doesn’t contain any secrets.
Deployment wasn’t without struggles. The DigitalOcean droplet only has about 1 GB of RAM, and it runs several projects at once, including a database, Caddy and Watchtower, so the containers started to fail.
To fix it, I set up a 2 GB swap file, which lets the server use part of the disk as extra memory when the RAM runs out. At the same time I added memory restrictions on each application and freed up over 200 MB and it now stable with around 550 MB usage of RAM.
summary: Deployment of the project, using GitHub Actions to run test and build maven project and Watchtower to poll for a new image to deploy.
title: seeCph: Deployment

content:
Finally, it was time to add security to the application. I started by configuring a token creator to determine what information to include, resulting in this setup:
JWT.create() .withIssuer(issuer) .withSubject(String.valueOf(user.id())) .withClaim("email", user.email()) .withClaim("name", user.name()) .withClaim("role", user.userRole().name()) .withIssuedAt(now) .withExpiresAt(now.plusMillis(expirationTime)) .sign(signingAlgorithm(secret)); The user role was particularly important, as I needed to enforce access control on my endpoints—ensuring, for example, that a standard user cannot modify events or delete other users. Getting this right took some effort because my codebase structure differed significantly from our class example. Most notably, the example used a String for roles, whereas I had already implemented mine using an Enum, but I managed to get it working smoothly in the end.
The values used to create the token, such as the secret key, issuer and token expiration time, are never hardcoded or committed. Locally they are read from a config.properties file that is listed in .gitignore. When deployed, the application reads the same values from environment variables instead. On the DigitalOcean server, Docker Compose loads them from a .env file and passes them to the container when it starts, so the Docker image itself contains no secrets. During the build, GitHub Actions gets the values it needs to run the tests from GitHub Secrets.
The setup for the login endpoint, along with the authentication and authorization handlers, came together quickly and cleanly:
public Javalin startServer(int port) { var app = Javalin.create(this::configuration); app.beforeMatched(securityHandler::authenticate); app.beforeMatched(securityHandler::authorize); // ... } Potential improvements for next time:
Allowing users to hold multiple roles.
Implementing token renewal or refresh mechanisms after a set period of activity.
Storing token identifiers to ensure tokens can be invalidated immediately upon logout or renewal.
I also integrated BCrypt for password hashing, which went smoothly since I have used it in previous projects. However, a new addition this time was implementing robust input validation using Context.bodyValidator() across user creation, login, updates, and password changes.
summary: Adding security features like creating JWT to users when they login, packed with the token itself, id, name, email and the very important user roles that gives access to different endpoint depending on the specific role. Passwords are hashed and sertified using BCrypt, making it more secure.
title: seeCph: Security

content:
RestAssured # After creating the endpoints, I needed to test if they actually worked as intended. I started by manually testing the connection with an HTTP test on localhost, just a quick positive test to see if it behaved as designed.
Next came the RestAssured tests to verify that my handlers returned the correct status codes across different scenarios, covering both positive and negative results. All of this helped ensure the application was working the way I planned.
Writing failure tests can be a bit tricky to get right, but as I worked through them, it got easier and easier. Since I had already tested my service layer, I had previously caught and corrected a few mistakes and behaviors in my code. The RestAssured tests mainly focused on validating my handlers’ contexts, which went pretty smoothly, though I did notice I needed better error and status handling in a few places.
Web-Hook # I also implemented a webhook to sync my API events once a day during off-hours at night, when server traffic is minimal. It is set up with GitHub Actions to hit this endpoint:
/api/v1/events/ticketmaster When sending a request to the endpoint, it also passes a key/password to check against a system environment variable before running the sync. This ensures it cannot be hit by unauthorized users. Once validated, it makes a new thread, running in the background, to run the syncs. This allows the main thread to immediately return a 200 OK status back to GitHub, preventing the HTTP request from timing out if the sync takes too long.
summary: Testing endpoints with RestAssured test with positive and negative test. Creating a webhook using GitHub Actions to hit endpoint, to activate daily syncs of my API events
title: seeCph: RestAssured

content:
Figuring out how to structure my code to handle my endpoints took a lot of time. The goal was to make the code readable and easy to maintain. Structuring it this way helps keep my classes aligned with the Single Responsibility Principle. For now, I ended up structuring it like this:
HTTP Request: User input
↓ Controller: Adds endpoints
↓ Handler: Manages user input validation & HTTP responses
↓ Service: Executes business logic
↓ DAO: Interacts with the database Handlers: Takes care of what happens when calling the different routes, manage user input validation using Javalin’s Validator, and set/return HTTP status messages. I will also implement a Logger here later on.
Controllers: Takes care of linking routes up with the methods in handlers. Here, I use Javalin’s EndpointGroup interface to add all routes in each controller.
Dependency Injection: To handle dependency injection, I created an ApplicationConfig class that makes sure DAOs, services, handlers, and controllers get what they need, and adds all controller endpoints in one method.
public class ApplicationConfig implements EndpointGroup { private final EventController eventController; private final UserController userController; private final AdvertController advertController; public ApplicationConfig(EntityManagerFactory emf) { // DAOs AdvertDAO advertDAO = new AdvertDAO(emf); EventDAO eventDAO = new EventDAO(emf); UserDAO userDAO = new UserDAO(emf); // Services EventService eventService = new EventService(eventDAO); UserService userService = new UserService(userDAO); AdvertService advertService = new AdvertService(advertDAO); // Handlers EventHandler eventHandler = new EventHandler(eventService); UserHandler userHandler = new UserHandler(userService); AdvertHandler advertHandler = new AdvertHandler(advertService); // Controllers this.eventController = new EventController(eventHandler); this.userController = new UserController(userHandler); this.advertController = new AdvertController(advertHandler); } @Override public void addEndpoints() { eventController.addEndpoints(); userController.addEndpoints(); advertController.addEndpoints(); } } If ApplicationConfig gets too big, the plan is to split it up into categories so it remains readable and easy to maintain.
To keep the code easier to maintain and build on, I use interfaces to provide a blueprint for new additions and keep method names consistent.
summary: Figuring out how to set up handlers, controllers and their endpoints. Handlers with javalins Validator and controllers with javalins EndPoint Group interface.
title: seeCph: Endpoints

content:
It’s was time to add API data, so have worked on setting up a call that gets data from Ticket Master and only events happening in Copenhagen, Denmark. Then using the received json file turn convert it to dto and then convert it to an entity, to persist it to the database.
Using ObjectMapper and @JsonIgnoreProperties is pretty new libaries to use. It makes it so much easier to fetch data and convert into dto.
For it to work, the dto classes / records have to be set up the right way, so it mirrors the data from json with the data you want. When setup right, it kinda feels like magic. Just make sure the dto “tree” starts from where you collect data.
It took some time to figure out exactly what data i wanted and how it should be represented in my entity. Cause I had to make it generic enough for it, to also work for other API’s and data fetching, while still getting relevant data to use.
Wished I used more time for groundwork to fugure out the variables for my Event entity.
Found an easy way to choose category from my ENUM directly when the dto is made, that makes it much easier in my service class TicketMasterConverter or any new ones. But also if I need to change anything it my ENUM I only have to do it in one place when I don’t have any switches.
@JsonCreator public static EventCategory fromLabel(String label) { if (label == null) return OTHERS; return events.getOrDefault(label.toLowerCase(), OTHERS); } And then every ENUM has String label to catch and give the right one.
summary: Fetching data from Ticket Master API and converting received json file into a DTO. After this using a converter to convert to entity and persist to databse.
title: seeCph: Ticket Master API

content:
This week was about finishing tests for my entity DAOs’ basic CRUD operations.
To make it possible to test properly, I needed to add exception handling to all CRUD operations. To make this easier and more future-proof, I added an abstract generic <T> class with all basic operations.
This will make it easier to maintain the code in the future, both when adding new entities or updating existing ones.
When writing the @Tests, I also updated my entities with overridden equals() and hashCode() methods to compare objects in the tests.
I also added @PrePersist and @PreUpdate methods to set certain variables based on others, which simplifies maintenance by keeping entity lifecycle logic directly in its own class.
@PrePersist private void prePersist() { this.status = !LocalDate.now().isBefore(startDate) && !LocalDate.now().isAfter(endDate); } @PreUpdate private void preUpdate() { this.status = LocalDate.now().isBefore(startDate) && !LocalDate.now().isAfter(endDate); } Refactoring with a generic abstract class with exception handling was challenging, but satisfying when it was done ✅
IntegrationTests for Event, Advert and all users took a big effort to keep track of all relations and getting them right. But it helped to find some flaws in my code, to persist, update and delete everything the way I wanted it to behave.
summary: This week was all about getting test-ready for basic CRUD operations across all DAOs. For that, I also needed to add exceptions to my DAO methods. I decided to do a big refactoring and create a generic jig with all basic CRUD operations for easier maintenance in the future.
title: seeCph: Testing and Refactoring DAOs
